name: Yohimbine

lead: Yohimbine comes from yohimbe bark and blocks alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, raising noradrenaline activity. Cutters use it, often with caffeine and fasted cardio, to release stubborn fat and get leaner in the face and midsection. It is a common ingredient in pre-workouts and fat burners.

Proponents say alpha-2 receptors in some fat depots resist fat release and blocking them promotes lipolysis. The studies found are small topical-fat trials from 1995 on women's thighs and research uses of the drug as a stress probe; none shows oral fat loss in dieting men. Its effect is short-lived, with a reported half-life under about an hour.

paras: It is taken fasted before cardio, usually in a pre-workout or fat-burner or alongside caffeine, during a cut. Users combine it with a calorie deficit and judge changes in stubborn areas over weeks.

Documented adverse effects include anxiety, high blood pressure, fast heart rate and gastrointestinal upset, with rare severe cases. It requires a prescription in some countries and is sold as a supplement in others.

chain: Raises fat release from stubborn areas
angle.text: Cutters use yohimbine, often with caffeine and fasted cardio, to release stubborn fat and get leaner in the face and midsection. It blocks alpha-2 receptors so more fat is mobilised from resistant areas. Support comes from mechanism and small studies; trials in dieting men are limited.

lead: Yohimbine is an indole alkaloid obtained from the bark of the West and Central African tree Pausinystalia johimbe (yohimbe). It acts as an antagonist at alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which raises norepinephrine release and sympathetic activity.[1][2][3] Bark extracts have been used in traditional West African medicine as a tonic and aphrodisiac, and yohimbine hydrochloride has been studied as a prescription drug for erectile dysfunction.[4][3][5]

In bodybuilding and cutting circles it is promoted as a fat-loss supplement to help leanness show in the face and midsection, particularly for "stubborn" fat and for use with fasted cardio. The reasoning is that alpha-2 receptors in some fat depots resist lipolysis and that blocking them releases that fat for use as fuel; it is an ingredient in many pre-workout and fat-burner products.[6][7][8][9][1][10]

Human research on body composition is small: a 1991 double-blind trial in obese women on a calorie-restricted diet, a 2006 randomised trial in professional soccer players, and 1995 trials of topical preparations on women's thighs.[10][6] Most other human work uses yohimbine as a research tool to provoke noradrenergic and stress responses.[11][12][13][14] Reported adverse effects include anxiety, raised blood pressure and heart rate, and gastrointestinal upset, and regulators in several countries restrict yohimbe supplements.[1][3][15]
infobox: Bark of Pausinystalia johimbe (yohimbe), also Aspidosperma quebracho-blanco [3]
Blocks presynaptic alpha-2 receptors, increasing norepinephrine release [2]
Yohimbine HCl; yohimbe bark extract; ingredient in pre-workouts and fat burners [9][3]
Varies: Rx-only in Canada and Australia; unscheduled in the US but not approved for health claims; yohimbe supplements banned in the UK [3]

paras: In the cutting and looksmaxxing context, yohimbine is used by already-lean dieters hoping to reduce residual body fat that resists loss, usually alongside caffeine and fasted training.[7][8][16] A Grokipedia summary says the proposed mechanism is strongest in fasted states and in areas rich in alpha-2 receptors such as the abdomen and thighs, and that forum users describe taking it before fasted cardio.[1] Reports are mixed; some find it helpful while others report jitters, anxiety or tolerance.[1]

A hypothesis paper by McCarty in 2002 proposed that pre-exercise yohimbine could raise lipolysis and free fatty acids during exercise and could synergise with caffeine; it presented no new experimental data.[10]

Yohimbe bark has long been used in West African traditional medicine as a tonic and aphrodisiac, and the species' bark is exported mainly from Cameroon for tinctures and supplements.[4] Yohimbine has been studied for erectile dysfunction, female sexual dysfunction and delayed ejaculation, with Wikipedia describing the evidence as insufficient or no better than placebo; reviews of erectile dysfunction treatments and natural aphrodisiacs discuss it.[3][17][18] It has also been investigated as an adjunct to exposure therapy for PTSD, and in veterinary medicine since the 1970s to reverse xylazine sedation.[3]

Wikipedia dates the naming of yohimbine to 1896, when Adolph Spiegel described the alkaloid extracted from yohimbe bark, and notes that German scientific interest grew around 1900 after a report of aphrodisiac effects.[3] The compound's identity was disputed for decades: two 1914 papers claimed it equalled quebrachine, and Effler and Effler used modern analytical methods in 1972 to confirm that the two are the same compound.[3] Witkop proposed the correct structure in 1943 and a team led by Eugene van Tamelen completed the first synthesis in 1958 in 23 steps.[3]

The alpha-adrenergic rationale for weight-loss use was developed through studies of presynaptic regulation of catecholamine release, reviewed in 1980, and Polish researchers published obesity trials of yohimbine from 1986 to 1991.[2][10] Dietary supplements in the United States are regulated under the 1994 DSHEA framework, and yohimbe-containing products entered the bodybuilding fat-burner market through that route, according to a Grokipedia summary.[1]

Yohimbine has high affinity for alpha-2 adrenoceptors, including the presynaptic autoreceptors that normally limit noradrenaline release, so it increases noradrenergic signalling.[2][1][3] It also binds with moderate affinity to alpha-1, several serotonin receptors and dopamine D2 receptors, and acts as a partial agonist at 5-HT1A.[3] Researchers use it as an experimental way to provoke noradrenergic and stress responses in humans and animals, for example in studies of anxiety, decision making and drug-cue reactivity.[11][12][13][14] It also increases salivary secretion in humans.[19]

Wikipedia reports oral bioavailability ranging from 7 to 86 percent (mean about 33 percent) and an elimination half-life of about 0.25 to 2.5 hours, with excretion in urine as metabolites.[3] A Grokipedia summary adds peak plasma levels around 45 minutes, metabolism mainly by CYP2D6 and a stimulant effect that adds to caffeine and ephedrine.[1]

A 1991 double-blind randomised trial by Kucio and colleagues gave 20 obese women either yohimbine or placebo for three weeks on a 1,000 kcal daily diet; the yohimbine group lost more weight (3.55 kg versus 2.21 kg), energy expenditure and sympathetic activity were maintained, and lipolysis was not significantly affected.[10] A companion study of 15 obese inpatients found no significant change in gastric emptying, and Polish trials in 1986 and 1990 reported on yohimbine in obesity.[10]

A 2006 randomised controlled trial by Ostojic gave 20 professional male soccer players yohimbine or an identical placebo daily for 21 days. Body mass and muscle mass did not change significantly, body fat percentage fell significantly in the yohimbine group, exercise performance did not change and no participant reported side effects; the author described it as potentially suitable as a fat-loss strategy in elite athletes.[10] A Grokipedia summary describes small fat-loss effects over 3 to 4 weeks in later reviews and notes no long-term studies, and says a 1995 trial found topical yohimbine ointment ineffective for thigh girth, while a later multi-ingredient lotion showed some benefit alongside diet and exercise.[1]

A 1995 report described three small trials in overweight women using one thigh as a double-blind control, including an ointment containing forskolin, yohimbine and aminophylline applied to the thigh alongside diet and walking.[6]

Other human studies use yohimbine as a research tool rather than a treatment: effects on action monitoring, approach-avoidance behaviour with hydrocortisone, pain perception and drug-cue reactivity.[12][11][20][13] A bioequivalence study of 5 mg tablets was registered in erectile dysfunction and a trial in type 2 diabetes patients with a genetic variant was also registered.[5][21] A systematic review of supplements in elite soccer players is listed in the literature, but its abstract does not report yohimbine findings.[22]

Reported adverse effects include anxiety, hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, tremor, nausea and gastrointestinal distress, with serious toxicity such as arrhythmia, seizures and myocardial infarction reported at high doses.[1][3] The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says yohimbine has been linked to irregular heartbeat, blood pressure problems, heart attacks and seizures, and cites a California Poison Control study in which yohimbe exposures caused stomach problems, rapid heartbeat, anxiety and high blood pressure, with callers more likely to need medical care than other callers.[15]

A case report describes yohimbine-induced bronchospasm, and a review of herb-drug interactions lists it among herbal products with interaction potential.[23][24] Wikipedia reports that interactions with prescription drugs can cause sudden hypotension, irregular heartbeat, heart failure and death, that benzodiazepines and barbiturates can reduce its anxiety effects and that imipramine can intensify them; NCCIH advises against use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors or tricyclic antidepressants and notes it may be unsafe in pregnancy or breastfeeding.[3][15]

sections.h: Product quality, legal status and regulation
paras: Cohen and colleagues analysed 49 US supplement brands labelled as containing yohimbe or yohimbine and found yohimbine per serving ranged from none detected to 12.1 mg, only 11 brands listed a quantity and most of those were inaccurate (23 to 147 percent of label), and 18 percent gave no adverse-effect information.[10] A 2024 analysis of weight-loss supplements sold near US military bases found 82 percent of 44 products had inaccurate labels, though the abstract does not name yohimbe.[10]

Wikipedia reports that yohimbine is unscheduled in the United States but that marketing an over-the-counter product with a health claim such as erectile dysfunction without FDA approval is illegal, and that the FDA has issued multiple warning letters to yohimbe supplement makers; it is prescription-only in Canada (yohimbe products were removed from the market in 2019) and Australia (Schedule 4), unlicensed in the UK where yohimbe herbal supplements are banned, and a 2013 EFSA opinion could not establish a safe health-based guidance value for supplements.[3] In 2022 the Tennessee Poison Center warned that over-the-counter yohimbine products could be fatal because of unregulated dosing.[3] The wild tree is reported to be over-exploited because harvesting its bark kills it.[3][4] A T Nation user notes that in their country products such as yohimbine require a prescription.[25] Grokipedia says WADA does not prohibit yohimbine.[1]

On looksmax.org, a thread titled as a "legit or cope" question asks whether yohimbine helps already-lean users reach single-digit body fat. Replies say it is in their pre-workout, that it makes fasted cardio more effective, and that excess makes users feel sick.[7] On T Nation, users list it in cutting stacks with caffeine, carnitine, ephedra-type stimulants and cardarine.[16][8][26] Reports describe strong stimulant effects including tingling, chills and a runny nose.[27][28] These are individual accounts; no dose guidance is given here.

lore.intro: Yohimbine is described in cutting forums as an add-on for lean bodybuilders targeting stubborn fat, usually with caffeine and fasted cardio.[7][16][8]

Eugene van Tamelen's team completes the first synthesis in 23 steps [3].
